key_insight: PoseBench systematically shows that modern deep-learning docking and structure‑prediction methods can achieve high accuracy on easy, rigid targets but struggle with receptor flexibility, novel chemotypes, and scoring discrimination — exposing concrete failure modes that limit real‑world applicability.
problem_solved: Provides a standardized, comprehensive benchmark to objectively evaluate and compare AI‑based protein–ligand docking and structure‑prediction methods, revealing strengths, weaknesses, and evaluation blind spots that previously hampered progress.
method: Assemble PoseBench: a curated, diverse dataset of protein–ligand complexes with annotated poses and difficulty labels.
Evaluate multiple state‑of‑the‑art deep‑learning docking and structure‑prediction models under uniform metrics (pose RMSD, success rates, scoring calibration) and controlled conditions.
Perform systematic failure‑mode analyses to identify model biases and recommend dataset, scoring, and modeling improvements.
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners clear, actionable diagnostics and benchmarks to prioritize improvements (e.g., handling receptor flexibility, improving scoring and generalization), accelerating reliable model development for structure‑based drug discovery.
visual_elements: Pipeline schematic: PoseBench construction → evaluation workflow → key metrics
Bar chart comparing methods by near‑native pose success rate (e.g., % ≤2 Å RMSD)
Scatter plot of pose accuracy versus ligand complexity or receptor flexibility to highlight failure regimes
Heatmap of failure modes by chemistry/target class, with simple protein and ligand icons
paper_title: Assessing the potential of deep learning for protein–ligand docking
paper_authors: Alex Morehead, Nabin Giri, Jian Liu, Pawan Neupane, Jianlin Cheng
